status: Ready: six core profiles; complementary craft profiles are maintained in craft.json
editorialNote: Original educational analysis of public sources. Descriptions of decisions distinguish documented choices from interpretation. Sources remain the property of their respective authors; inclusion implies no endorsement.

people.name: Ryo Lu
people.focus: Composable product systems, contextual AI, and human agency
people.keyIdea: Make AI useful through the product's existing objects and contexts, while preserving the user's ability to understand and reshape the system.

artifacts.title: The design thinking behind Notion AI
artifacts.author: Ryo Lu
artifacts.summary: A historical account of integrating AI horizontally across Notion's blocks, packaging common tasks, and changing available actions according to the current page and selection.

artifacts.title: ryOS
artifacts.author: Ryo Lu / ryOS contributors
artifacts.summary: A desktop-like environment with a persistent virtual filesystem, multiple applications, and an assistant. Read the architecture as an inspectable product artifact, not as proof that its interaction model is superior.

artifacts.title: augmenting human intellect
artifacts.author: Ryo Lu
artifacts.summary: Argues for AI tools that increase people's understanding, expression, and control, rather than measuring progress solely by unattended output.

decisions.decision: Package common AI actions while retaining a customizable underlying system.
decisions.alternative: Expose only an unrestricted prompt or only fixed single-purpose features.
decisions.tradeoff: Defaults lower the entry cost; customization preserves flexibility but adds concepts and maintenance.

decisions.decision: Use page and selection state to prioritize drafting, continuing, extracting, or editing.
decisions.alternative: Show the same global AI menu everywhere.
decisions.tradeoff: Context reduces repeated explanation; context mistakes can hide the action a person wants.
decisions.status: Documented product decision; downside is analysis

decisions.decision: Give the assistant shared application and file context inside a persistent environment.
decisions.alternative: Make chat the only place work exists.
decisions.tradeoff: Stable objects can support continuity; a desktop metaphor introduces navigation and coordination costs.
decisions.status: Observed artifact structure; tradeoff is analysis

decisions.decision: Evaluate empowerment through what the person can understand and change.
decisions.alternative: Optimize only the volume of work performed without the person.
decisions.tradeoff: Meaningful participation may require interaction time that a pure automation metric would count as overhead.

writingTechniques.technique: Move from foundational model to concrete states.
writingTechniques.evidence: The Notion essay first explains blocks, then walks through empty pages, populated pages, selections, and database use.

writingTechniques.technique: Use historical contrast to sharpen a present choice.
writingTechniques.evidence: The augmentation essay links earlier human-computer ideas to a current distinction between participating in thought and waiting for output.

writingTechniques.technique: Turn an abstraction into inspectable structure.
writingTechniques.evidence: The ryOS README enumerates applications, persistent storage, and project directories rather than describing the product only with a slogan.

exercise.task: Choose a repeated workflow. Define five durable object types and three meaningful states for each. Design contextual AI actions for two states, plus an escape hatch for a custom request.
exercise.deliverable: An object map, two interactive screens, and a decision log explaining which context the AI receives.
evaluation: Can another person predict the action from the selected object?
Can they compare, revise, and undo the result?
Can they explain what changed without reopening a transcript?

limitations: The Notion article describes a 2023 design, not the current product specification.
The ryOS repository was read, not installed or functionally tested.
The augmentation essay is a normative argument, not an empirical outcome study.
people.coverage: Three primary artifacts reviewed: one product essay, one repository README, one personal essay. Product decisions and analyst interpretations are labeled.

people.name: Amelia Wattenberger
people.focus: Explorable explanations, human-AI interfaces, and tools for thought
people.keyIdea: Use AI to create manipulable models of a problem, not merely more prose for the user to review.

artifacts.title: Why Chatbots Are Not the Future
artifacts.author: Amelia Wattenberger
artifacts.summary: Identifies weak affordances, repeated context entry, isolated answers, and forced generation-review switching as limitations of plain chat.

artifacts.title: Code was our medium for thought
artifacts.author: Amelia Wattenberger
artifacts.summary: Explores the loss of mental models when code production accelerates beyond understanding, and proposes editable playgrounds for reasoning about a product.

artifacts.title: Chat is AI's command line
artifacts.author: Amelia Wattenberger
artifacts.summary: Uses a travel-planning example to explore direct manipulation, dependent updates, undo, and visible work state alongside conversational direction.

artifacts.title: Code Atlas
artifacts.author: Amelia Wattenberger, credited by GitHub Next
artifacts.summary: A prototype represents model-generated solutions as executable connected code blocks and editable inputs. The project page explicitly labels it an early exploration.

artifacts.title: Bridging the hard and the soft
artifacts.author: Amelia Wattenberger
artifacts.summary: Develops a framework for combining dependable structure with adaptive content and workflows at multiple scales.

decisions.decision: Keep a persistent editable working artifact instead of producing detached answers.
decisions.alternative: Append a fresh full response for each requested change.
decisions.tradeoff: Continuity makes changes easier to inspect; it requires a coherent editing and version model.

decisions.decision: Expose inputs and intermediate structure as an editable workflow.
decisions.alternative: Return a polished answer without a model the person can manipulate.
decisions.tradeoff: A visible model supports debugging and learning; generated structure can still be wrong and needs validation.

decisions.decision: Let direct edits update dependent constraints and keep work status beside the object.
decisions.alternative: Translate every small adjustment into another textual instruction.
decisions.tradeoff: This suits spatial and relational tasks but can be expensive to generalize across arbitrary requests.

decisions.decision: Combine fixed modules with flexible generated elements instead of treating rigidity and adaptability as a binary.
decisions.alternative: Either hard-code the complete workflow or generate the whole interface.
decisions.tradeoff: Boundaries can provide reliable behavior; the designer must decide where variation remains understandable.

writingTechniques.technique: Make the reader experience the argument.
writingTechniques.evidence: The newer essays place controls and editable examples next to claims about manipulation and exploration.

writingTechniques.technique: Show a causal sequence rather than only a conclusion.
writingTechniques.evidence: The code essay walks through research, implementation, observation, and revision before explaining what that cycle taught the developer.

writingTechniques.technique: Carry one metaphor across several scales.
writingTechniques.evidence: Hard and soft materials frame distinctions between content, components, modules, and whole workflows.

exercise.task: Take one AI-generated plan. Build a small editable model with three controls, dependencies, undo, and one intentionally invalid state. Compare it with a chat-only version.
exercise.deliverable: A working explorable explanation and a short comparison using the same task.
evaluation: Can a learner predict a change before making it?
Can they locate and correct the invalid assumption?
Does the interface preserve understanding after several revisions?

limitations: The essays are arguments and prototypes, not controlled comparisons establishing that chat always loses.
Code Atlas is a 2023 early-stage exploration; its claims about contemporary model limitations must be read historically.
The interactive pages were inspected through their published text and controls, not comprehensively usability-tested.
people.coverage: Five primary artifacts reviewed, spanning critique, prototype, historical analogy, and a structural design framework. Unknown publication dates are left unspecified.

people.name: Karri Saarinen
people.focus: Product coherence, design leadership, and the human-agent workbench
people.keyIdea: A coherent product provides the context for powerful tools; generating a plausible interface is not the same as resolving the problem.

artifacts.title: A design reset (part I)
artifacts.author: Karri Saarinen
artifacts.summary: Makes the case for addressing accumulated design debt through a coordinated reset tied to the product's direction.

artifacts.title: How we redesigned the Linear UI (part II)
artifacts.author: Karri Saarinen and three coauthors; sections have individual bylines
artifacts.summary: Documents concept exploration and implementation of a redesign. Saarinen's section explains why navigation changes were excluded to control scope and risk.

artifacts.title: Design for the AI age
artifacts.author: Karri Saarinen
artifacts.summary: Argues for a structured application as a workbench where people direct, inspect, and approve agent work.

artifacts.title: Output isn't design
artifacts.author: Karri Saarinen
artifacts.summary: Distinguishes producing form from understanding context and resolving conflicting needs, constraints, and edge cases.

decisions.decision: Exclude navigation redesign from an otherwise broad UI reset.
decisions.alternative: Change application chrome and information architecture together.
decisions.tradeoff: Lower engineering and habit-disruption risk at the cost of leaving a known problem for later.

decisions.decision: Explore complete screens and flows before converging on a visual direction.
decisions.alternative: Resolve isolated components without testing their fit across the product.
decisions.tradeoff: Cross-product coherence requires more exploration; it can surface relationships missed by local optimization.

decisions.decision: Tie a design reset to a larger product shift and leadership commitment.
decisions.alternative: Treat it as discretionary visual polish.
decisions.tradeoff: Strategic sponsorship enables cross-team changes but concentrates influence and requires explicit scope safeguards.
decisions.status: Author's management recommendation; downside is analysis

decisions.decision: Keep agent operation inside a structured work environment.
decisions.alternative: Rely on generic conversation and disconnected exports.
decisions.tradeoff: Persistent context and review fit repeated workflows; a dedicated workbench may be excessive for one-off questions.

writingTechniques.evidence: The redesign series separates why a reset matters from how the team approached the actual work.

writingTechniques.technique: Use a concrete spatial metaphor to explain an abstract system.
writingTechniques.evidence: The workbench makes the relationship between application context, AI tools, and human review easier to picture.

writingTechniques.technique: Define the mistaken assumption before offering the distinction.
writingTechniques.evidence: Output isn't design begins with production-centric tool promises, then reframes design around fit between form and context.

exercise.task: Audit a mature workflow for design debt. Propose a reset, then explicitly exclude one tempting but high-risk change. Draw three complete flows, including an edge case.
exercise.deliverable: A one-page reset proposal, a scope exclusion, three linked flows, and a risk register.
evaluation: Is the change tied to a user or product need rather than fashion?
Can the team explain why the excluded change was deferred?

limitations: The redesign case study is multi-author; implementation details must not all be attributed to Saarinen.
The essays reflect a founder-led product organization and do not prove the same process fits every company.
Recommendations about redesign cadence or short-term metrics are the author's perspective, not universal empirical laws.
people.coverage: Four primary artifacts reviewed, with individual authorship distinguished from the multi-author case study.

people.name: Steve Ruiz
people.focus: Canvas interaction engineering, measurable details, and shared human-AI surfaces
people.keyIdea: Make invisible interaction behavior observable, then encode intentional tolerances and stable rules.

artifacts.title: Text is not enough
artifacts.author: Steve Ruiz
artifacts.summary: Shows where an editable canvas can supplement chat for visual and abstract reasoning; explicitly acknowledges that chat works well for many tasks.

artifacts.title: An exhaustive review of design tool hover areas
artifacts.author: Steve Ruiz
artifacts.summary: Maps cursor behavior across a grid to expose hidden resize and rotation hit areas in design tools, making conventions measurable rather than assumed.

artifacts.title: Debugging a physical race condition with modifier keys
artifacts.author: Steve Ruiz and Ani Krishnan
artifacts.summary: Explains why nominally simultaneous keyboard and mouse releases can cancel a drag modifier and describes a short release tolerance.

artifacts.title: Engineering imperfection with draw shapes
artifacts.author: Steve Ruiz
artifacts.summary: Uses seeded pseudorandomness and geometry-aware constraints to give shapes a hand-drawn character without unstable render-to-render jitter.

decisions.decision: Visualize interaction hit areas with a systematic sampling tool.
decisions.alternative: Infer conventions by cautiously moving a pointer and relying on memory.
decisions.tradeoff: Instrumentation makes discrepancies visible but captures only the sampled platform, state, and time.

decisions.decision: Delay modifier release by 150 ms in the described drag interaction.
decisions.alternative: Immediately apply every key-up event regardless of user intent.
decisions.tradeoff: Tolerance avoids accidental last-moment cancellation; too much delay would feel sticky.

decisions.decision: Seed imperfections from stable shape IDs.
decisions.alternative: Generate new random offsets on every render.
decisions.tradeoff: Stable variation preserves identity through edits; it requires deterministic handling of geometry and seeds.

decisions.decision: Make visual explanations editable by both human and agent.
decisions.alternative: Exchange screenshots or textual descriptions without a shared model.
decisions.tradeoff: Direct reference improves steering for visual work; an extra canvas can be unnecessary for simple exchanges.
decisions.status: Documented product capability; tradeoff is analysis

writingTechniques.technique: Begin with a tiny observable failure and trace its mechanism.
writingTechniques.evidence: The modifier article starts with an effect disappearing at release, explains event ordering, and only then presents the timeout.

writingTechniques.technique: Use the naive implementation as a foil.
writingTechniques.evidence: The imperfection essay shows why fresh random values fail before introducing stable seeded variation.

writingTechniques.technique: Make a comparison reproducible in concept.
writingTechniques.evidence: The hover investigation states its grid-sampling method before presenting tool-by-tool observations.

exercise.task: Find an interaction that fails under rapid or imprecise input. Instrument it, collect an event trace, and compare immediate response with a small intent-preserving tolerance.
exercise.deliverable: A reproducible failing case, an event timeline, and two working variants with a justified threshold.
evaluation: Does the change fix the failure without blocking intentional reversal?
Can the failure be reproduced rather than merely described?
Have keyboard and pointer paths both been tested?

limitations: The modifier article is coauthored with Ani Krishnan.
The reported 150 ms value is specific to the described interaction, not a universal timing rule.
The hover survey is a snapshot of sampled tools, not evidence about all versions or platforms.
No claim is made that canvases should replace chat everywhere.
people.coverage: Four primary artifacts reviewed, combining interaction research, two technical case studies, and an AI work-surface demonstration.

people.name: Brian Lovin
people.focus: Fast experiments, critique, and evidence-producing AI workflows
people.keyIdea: Make a workflow produce evidence of its own quality, and document what actually changed your mind.

artifacts.title: Give your agent a laboratory
artifacts.author: Brian Lovin
artifacts.summary: Reframes vague requests as instrumented loops with baselines, hypotheses, tests, visual comparison, and reports.

artifacts.title: Give your agent a laboratory, pt. II
artifacts.author: Brian Lovin
artifacts.summary: Describes experiments on newsletter extraction and audio transcription. Reported cost and speed results are specific to his implementation and benchmark.

artifacts.title: Design critique for fun and profit
artifacts.author: Brian Lovin
artifacts.summary: Explains revisions to pricing, scope, and positioning after delivering early critique projects, including reputational concerns and distribution advantages.

artifacts.title: My playbook for shipping side projects
artifacts.author: Brian Lovin
artifacts.summary: Proposes explicit shipping thresholds, ongoing communication, and clear onboarding for people arriving without launch context.

decisions.decision: Require an observable baseline and verification loop before optimization.
decisions.alternative: Ask an agent to make an application faster or prettier without measurable acceptance criteria.
decisions.tradeoff: Instrumentation costs time but helps distinguish improvement from persuasive claims.

decisions.decision: Benchmark combinations rather than assume which processing step will help.
decisions.alternative: Choose a library or model through intuition alone.
decisions.tradeoff: Search can expose surprising options, but a weak benchmark can optimize the wrong outcome.

decisions.decision: Reframe critique around a useful deliverable rather than a fixed hourly promise.
decisions.alternative: Sell a narrowly timed visual cleanup regardless of what the product needs.
decisions.tradeoff: Outcome framing supports depth but requires careful scope and expectations.

decisions.decision: Give direct-to-article visitors contextual onboarding.
decisions.alternative: Assume every reader saw the homepage or launch announcement.
decisions.tradeoff: A conditional introduction aids newcomers while avoiding repeated interruption for returning visitors.

writingTechniques.technique: Use before-and-after requests to teach a mental model.
writingTechniques.evidence: The laboratory essay contrasts vague requests with phased, testable workflows.

writingTechniques.technique: Publish the correction, not just the apparent success.
writingTechniques.evidence: The critique retrospective explains what he changed about pricing, scope, and tone after the initial launch.

writingTechniques.technique: Connect a general recommendation to a specific product repair.
writingTechniques.evidence: The side-project essay grounds its warning about context-free visitors in the conditional banner added to Staff Design.

exercise.task: Choose a small product defect. Define a baseline and a quality rubric before asking an agent to improve it. Require three hypotheses and an evidence-backed comparison.
exercise.deliverable: A benchmark or visual test set, a before/after report, and a short retrospective about one rejected approach.
evaluation: Can someone reproduce the claimed improvement?
Does the rubric cover failure cases rather than only the happy path?
Are human judgments separated from measured results?

limitations: The reports are first-person accounts; underlying benchmarks were not independently reproduced.
The audio speed and cost findings must not be generalized to other speech, languages, models, or billing systems.
The consulting experiment benefited from an existing audience and does not establish a universal pricing strategy.
people.coverage: Four first-person artifacts reviewed, including two workflow reports, a critique retrospective, and a side-project practice essay.

people.name: Josh Puckett
people.focus: Live interface tuning, browser detail, and transmitting craft judgment
people.keyIdea: Shorten the loop between a felt mismatch and a directly adjustable parameter, and preserve the reasons behind craft decisions.

artifacts.title: DialKit
artifacts.author: Josh Puckett, credited on the product page
artifacts.sourceType: Original tool, documentation, and interactive examples
artifacts.summary: A live control surface for tuning interface parameters, spring or easing behavior, and timelines. Documentation distinguishes development use from optional production exposure.

artifacts.title: Seamless Backgrounds on Mobile Safari
artifacts.author: Josh Puckett
artifacts.summary: Explains a fixed-edge color technique for browser chrome and documents why a theme-color tag alone did not satisfy the author's desired effect.

artifacts.title: On Being An Elder
artifacts.author: Josh Puckett
artifacts.summary: Argues that experienced practitioners should preserve judgment and mistakes, create opportunities, remain available, and keep learning.

decisions.decision: Expose meaningful visual parameters through live controls.
decisions.alternative: Repeatedly edit code or reprompt to compare small visual adjustments.
decisions.tradeoff: Immediate exploration encourages comparisons, but poorly chosen knobs can distract from the underlying product problem.
decisions.status: Observed tool design; tradeoff is analysis

decisions.decision: Hide the tuning interface in production by default.
decisions.alternative: Ship development controls into every end-user experience.
decisions.tradeoff: The development environment stays powerful without adding accidental production complexity; deliberate public demos can opt in.

decisions.decision: Use separately controlled solid top and bottom edge colors for the targeted Safari effect.
decisions.alternative: Rely only on one theme-color value.
decisions.tradeoff: It supports different edge colors but cannot faithfully extend arbitrary imagery or a horizontally varying gradient.

decisions.decision: Teach the judgment behind a practice rather than preserve the practice as an unquestionable rule.
decisions.alternative: Transmit seniority as authority or copy historical techniques without context.
decisions.tradeoff: Reasons and mistakes take more work to document, but help later practitioners adapt rather than imitate.

writingTechniques.technique: Anticipate the obvious solution and show its boundary.
writingTechniques.evidence: The Safari article raises the theme-color alternative before explaining why it did not meet the specific requirement.

writingTechniques.technique: Pair minimal examples with named limitations.
writingTechniques.evidence: The Safari article progresses from default behavior to a simple fix, dynamic colors, and an explicit limitations section.

writingTechniques.technique: Translate a value into concrete responsibilities.
writingTechniques.evidence: The elder essay uses action-led sections and specific mentoring experiences instead of leaving its argument at a general appeal to generosity.

exercise.task: Take one modal or transition and expose only four meaningful controls. Save three variants, then write the reasoning behind the preferred one and one platform limitation.
exercise.deliverable: A small live tuning demo, three named presets, and a 250-word decision note.
evaluation: Do the controls correspond to meaningful perceptual differences?
Does the chosen result still work with reduced motion and keyboard interaction?
Could another designer reproduce the judgment from the note?

limitations: DialKit documentation was read; the tool was not installed or benchmarked.
The Safari behavior is browser-version-dependent and should be rechecked on target devices.
The elder essay provides values and examples, not evidence of measured organizational outcomes.
people.coverage: Three primary artifacts reviewed: an original tool, a browser implementation essay, and a reflective practice essay.
